title: AI Therapy Apps in 2024: Do They Actually Work?
description: A critical look at AI-powered mental health apps like Woebot, Wysa, and ChatGPT for therapy. What the research shows, their limitations, and when they might help.
author: HeyPsych Editorial Team

content.text: AI chatbots that provide therapy-like support have exploded in popularity. Millions now use apps like Woebot, Wysa, and even general AI assistants for mental health support. But do they actually help? And when might they cause harm?
The Current Landscape of AI Mental Health Apps
AI therapy apps fall into several categories:

items: Purpose-built therapeutic chatbots (Woebot, Wysa, Youper)
AI companions and support (Replika, Character.AI)
General AI assistants used for mental health (ChatGPT, Claude)
AI-augmented human therapy platforms (Talkspace AI features)

content.text: What the Research Shows
Woebot
A Stanford RCT found Woebot reduced depression symptoms (PHQ-9) by 22% over two weeks compared to an information-only control group.
content.citation: Fitzpatrick et al., JMIR Mental Health, 2017

content.text: Woebot uses CBT principles and has the most research behind it. However, most studies are short-term (2-8 weeks) and funded by the company.
Wysa

Wysa has shown effectiveness for depression, anxiety, and workplace stress in multiple studies. A 2023 randomized trial found significant improvements in depression and anxiety compared to waitlist controls.
General AI (ChatGPT, Claude)

No controlled studies exist on using general AI assistants for therapy. While they can provide supportive conversations and information, they're not designed for mental health care and lack safety guardrails.
What AI Therapy Apps Do Well

items: Available 24/7 when human support isn't accessible
No waitlists or scheduling barriers
Reduced stigma—easier for some to open up to a bot
Consistent delivery of evidence-based techniques (CBT, DBT skills)
Affordable or free compared to traditional therapy
Good for learning coping skills and psychoeducation

content.text: Critical Limitations
AI chatbots cannot diagnose conditions, prescribe medication, handle crisis situations appropriately, or provide the human connection essential to therapeutic healing.
Key limitations include:

items: No true understanding of context or complex emotions
Cannot adapt to nuanced clinical presentations
Risk of missing serious symptoms or crisis signals
May reinforce unhelpful patterns if not carefully designed
Privacy concerns with sensitive mental health data
Lack of accountability when things go wrong

content.text: When AI Therapy Might Help
AI apps may be most useful for:

items: Learning CBT or DBT skills between therapy sessions
Mild symptoms of anxiety or depression
Stress management and wellness maintenance
Initial support while waiting for human care
People in areas with no mental health providers
Supplementing (not replacing) traditional therapy

content.text: When to Choose Human Therapy Instead

items: Moderate to severe depression or anxiety
Suicidal thoughts or self-harm
Trauma and PTSD
Complex mental health conditions
When medication might be needed
Relationship or interpersonal issues
When previous AI app use hasn't helped

content.text: The Privacy Question
Mental health data is extremely sensitive. Before using any AI therapy app, consider:

items: What data is collected and stored?
Is the data used to train AI models?
Who has access to your conversations?
What happens if the company is sold or goes bankrupt?
Is the app HIPAA compliant? (Most are not)

content.text: Our Assessment of Major Apps
Woebot
Best evidence base. Good for CBT skill-building. Can feel robotic. Best for: Learning coping skills, mild anxiety/depression.
Wysa
More conversational feel. Includes meditation and journaling. Good research support. Best for: General emotional support, workplace stress.
Youper
Focuses on emotional tracking. Uses AI for personalization. Less research than others. Best for: Mood tracking with guided support.
The Bottom Line

AI therapy apps can be a helpful supplement for mental health—but they're not a replacement for human care. The best evidence supports using them for skill-building and mild symptoms. If your symptoms are moderate or severe, or if you're in crisis, seek human support through a therapist, psychiatrist, or crisis line.
Think of AI therapy apps like mental health vitamins—they might help maintain wellness, but you need actual medicine for serious conditions.
